learn.title: How Rooftop Solar Works and Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar transforms buildings into power generators, helping India meet its 280 GW renewable target by 2030. Net metering allows surplus energy to be shared with the grid, reducing costs and enabling energy independence for households and businesses.
learn.c1_text: Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight into electricity via the photoelectric effect. A typical rooftop system (3kW) generates 4-5 units/day, sufficient for a 3-4 family home. Panels use silicon semiconductors to release electrons when hit by photons.
learn.c2_text: Net metering credits excess solar power fed back into the grid. India's 2016 policy allows consumers to offset consumption with surplus generation. For every unit exported, one unit is drawn from the grid, billed at regulated rates.
learn.c3_text: MNRE supports 40 GW rooftop solar by 2022. States like Gujarat and Maharashtra lead with net metering policies. Over 5.5 GW rooftop solar was installed by 2023, with subsidies up to 30% for residential systems.
learn.stat3: 30% capital subsidy for residential rooftop systems

learn.title: Solar PV Panels: The Photoelectric Effect Explained
learn.intro: Solar PV panels harness sunlight's energy through the photoelectric effect, a quantum phenomenon discovered by Einstein. This process converts light into electricity without moving parts, making solar power a clean, silent alternative to fossil fuels.
learn.c1_text: When photons strike a solar cell, they knock electrons free, creating a flow of electricity. This quantum effect works best with silicon cells, which have a bandgap of 1.1 eV. A single photon can liberate one electron, generating current.
learn.c2_text: PV cells use doped silicon layers: n-type (extra electrons) and p-type (electron holes). An electric field at the junction pushes electrons toward the front contact. Cells are wired into panels, with bypass diodes preventing shading losses. Efficiency ranges from 15-22% for commercial panels.
learn.c3_text: The US DOE notes solar PV capacity reached 200 GW globally by 2023. In the US, solar provides 3.5% of electricity. Silicon's abundance and improving cell technologies like PERC and TOPCon are driving cost declines from $400/W in 2010 to $0.30/W in 2024.

learn.title: Sodium-Ion Batteries: Affordable Alternative to Lithium-Ion
learn.intro: Sodium-ion batteries offer a cost-effective solution for grid-scale storage, addressing lithium's supply chain vulnerabilities. With abundant raw materials and similar performance, sodium-ion technology is revolutionizing energy storage economics for renewable integration and electric mobility.
learn.c1_text: Sodium-ion batteries use sodium ions instead of lithium, with comparable energy density (150-250 Wh/kg). Sodium is 100x more abundant in Earth's crust than lithium. Production costs are 30% lower due to cheaper raw materials like sodium carbonate and iron-based cathodes.
learn.c2_text: These batteries use Prussian blue analog cathodes and hard carbon anodes. They operate at 3.6V with cycle lives exceeding 2,000 cycles. While energy density lags behind lithium-ion, their thermal stability and fast-charging capability (0-80% in 15 mins) make them ideal for stationary storage.
learn.c3_text: IRENA reports sodium-ion projects in China's Jiangxi province and CATL's 30 GWh annual capacity by 2025. India's National Mission on Strategic and Critical Materials prioritizes sodium-ion R&D. Cost projections show sodium-ion batteries reaching $80/kWh by 2030, undercutting lithium-ion's $100/kWh.

learn.title: How Wind Turbines Generate Electricity
learn.intro: Wind turbines convert kinetic energy from moving air into clean electricity through aerodynamics and electromagnetic induction. Modern turbines can power 1,500 homes annually, making wind energy a cornerstone of India's 500 GW non-fossil fuel target by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Turbine blades act like airplane wings, creating lift as wind flows over curved surfaces. This generates rotational force (torque) at the blade tips moving 50-200 RPM. The optimal tip-speed ratio of 6-8 ensures maximum energy capture from variable wind speeds between 3-25 m/s.
learn.c2_text: The rotating shaft drives a gearbox increasing speed to 1,500-1,800 RPM for synchronous generators. These use electromagnetic induction: rotating magnets create alternating current in stator coils. Variable-speed turbines use power electronics to convert AC to DC and back to grid-compatible AC.
learn.c3_text: India's 60 GW wind capacity (2023) is concentrated in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Rajasthan. Offshore projects like Tamil Nadu's 850 MW initiative aim to tap stronger monsoon winds. Modern 3 MW turbines can generate 4.5 million kWh/year, enough for 1,500 homes with 20% capacity factor.
learn.stat3: 20% capacity factor for Indian wind farms
learn.stat4: 850 MW Tamil Nadu offshore wind project

learn.title: India's EV Policy: PM e-DRIVE and State Schemes
learn.intro: India's electric vehicle revolution is driven by PM e-DRIVE and state policies aiming for 30% EV sales by 2030. With $2.5 billion in incentives and 10,000 charging stations planned, the policy framework addresses imports, local manufacturing, and sustainable battery management.
learn.c1_text: Launched in 2023, PM e-DRIVE offers subsidies up to 15% for EV purchases and 25% for charging infrastructure. It targets 30% EV adoption in public transport and 50% in government fleets by 2030. The scheme includes tax exemptions for EV components and raw materials.
learn.c2_text: States like Maharashtra provide 100% registration tax waivers for EVs. Kerala offers 100% subsidy for home charging points. Delhi's FAME II phase II allocates $300 million for e-rickshaws and buses. These policies create a $2.5 billion incentive pool for EV adoption and infrastructure development.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 30% EV sales by 2030, requiring 7.5 million EVs on roads. NITI Aayog projects 1 million charging stations by 2030. The FAME II scheme has sanctioned 6,000 e-rickshaws and 600 electric buses. Battery swapping networks in cities like Delhi support rapid charging solutions.

learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation in India
learn.intro: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) mandates DISCOMs to source specific renewable energy percentages, driving India's clean energy transition. With RPOs rising to 24% by 2030, DISCOMs must balance grid reliability with sustainability targets under MNRE's regulatory framework.
learn.c1_text: RPO requires DISCOMs to purchase 25.56% renewable energy by 2030, increasing from 23.11% in 2023. It applies to central, state, anditage electricity distribution companies. Non-compliance incurs penalties up to Rs. 1,000/kWh shortfall. RPOs include procurement from renewable generators and renewable energy certificates (RECs).
learn.c2_text: DISCOMs face financial stress from cross-subsidy subsidies and delayed payments. To meet RPO, they purchase RECs (certified renewable units) or enter PPAs with developers. As of 2023, 23.11% RPO compliance is achieved, with 15.4% from solar and 7.7% from wind. Stranded coal assets complicate transition timelines.
learn.c3_text: MNRE's latest RPO guidelines (2023) tighten compliance with quarterly monitoring. States like Gujarat and Tamil Nadu exceed targets via large solar parks. India's 100% electrification (2018) and RPO-driven solar growth (35 GW added in 2023) demonstrate policy effectiveness. REC trading volumes reached 12 GWh in FY2023-24.
